curriculum.lesson_evidence: Dance is part of every culture and often shows celebrations, stories, work or beliefs. Examples include Scottish Highland dancing, Irish step dancing, Greek circle dances, Indian classical and folk dances, Samoan and Tongan dances and kapa haka from Aotearoa New Zealand. Each tradition has its own steps, clothing, music and meaning. Some dances are sacred or restricted, so they are only for particular people or occasions. Learn about a cultural dance from a published source, a teacher or a community member who is happy to share it, and name where it comes from. Never mock or change a dance.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Choose a cultural dance and describe two things you can see (formation, steps, speed), where it is from and one respectful action before learning more.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'In an Irish step dance the dancers keep their arms by their sides and make quick, light steps with their feet. It is from Ireland. A respectful action is to use a source chosen by my teacher and say where the dance comes from.' It describes elements, names the origin and shows respect.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that all dances from the same culture are the same, or that any dance can be copied for fun. Each dance has its own meaning, and some are only for particular people, so we ask and learn from the right sources.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
With an adult, choose two cultural dances from a library book or approved website. For each write the place it comes from, two things you can see and one question you would ask a person from that community. Do not copy sacred or restricted dances.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teaching.feedback: Strong answer: 'In an Irish step dance the dancers keep their arms by their sides and make quick, light steps with their feet. It is from Ireland. A respectful action is to use a source chosen by my teacher and say where the dance comes from.' It describes elements, names the origin and shows respect.
teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Describe why the warned-against choice weakens the work, then write a stronger choice with a reason.
teaching.misconception: Changing the decoration without changing the artistic idea does not fix the error. Thinking that all dances from the same culture are the same, or that any dance can be copied for fun. Each dance has its own meaning, and some are only for particular people, so we ask and learn from the right sources.
teaching.model: Thinking that all dances from the same culture are the same, or that any dance can be copied for fun. Each dance has its own meaning, and some are only for particular people, so we ask and learn from the right sources. Here is a more helpful example: Example: Ravi watches a short video of a Greek circle dance chosen by his teacher. He writes: 'The dancers hold hands in a line that curves into a circle. The steps are in time with the music and the group moves together. It comes from Greece and is often danced at celebrations.' He names the formation, the time and the origin, and does not guess the meaning of any parts he does not know.
teaching.rule: Use an intentionally weak or disrespectful arts choice as a comparison. Name the specific error, then show a clearer or more respectful choice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same arts idea as the model, but with different content or material.
teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Make or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your main choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: Dance is part of every culture and often shows celebrations, stories, work or beliefs. Examples include Scottish Highland dancing, Irish step dancing, Greek circle dances, Indian classical and folk dances, Samoan and Tongan dances and kapa haka from Aotearoa New Zealand. Each tradition has its own steps, clothing, music and meaning. Some dances are sacred or restricted, so they are only for particular people or occasions. Learn about a cultural dance from a published source, a teacher or a community member who is happy to share it, and name where it comes from. Never mock or change a dance. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.
